analysis.title: Global Insolvencies Outlook 2028: Higher rates, higher energy bills, higher insolvencies
key_insights: Allianz's Global Insolvency Index is set to rise +5% in 2026, the fourth straight annual increase, after +6% in 2025 and +10% in 2024. It would sit 21% above the 2016-2019 average and about 4% below the GFC level. This is a +0.3pp upward revision to the prior estimate.

North America and Asia-Pacific make up 79% of the global rise. North America alone is 51%, partly because it holds 28% of global GDP and 33% of the headline index. The US accelerates to +12% from +7% in 2025, while Canada falls -3%.

Asia-Pacific contributes 28% of the 2026 increase (+2.6% regionally). Taiwan (+36%), South Korea (+12%) and Japan (+6%) rise, China is near flat (+1%), and Singapore drops -23%. Western Europe contributes 15% (+4%), led by Germany (+8%) and France (+3%).

24 of 44 monitored countries see rising insolvencies in 2026 and 30 exceed their 2016-2019 averages, up from 29 in 2025. The largest relative increases are Taiwan (+36%), Switzerland (+32%), Türkiye (+31%), Greece (+26%), Chile (+15%) and Russia (+14%). The largest absolute increases are Switzerland (+3,660), the US (+3,059), France (+2,312) and Germany (+1,836).

Major insolvencies (firms with turnover above EUR50mn) hit a record 376 in the first three quarters of 2026, 38 above the 2024 full-period peak and about one every 18 hours. Q3 2026 alone had 129. Retail (69), services (62) and construction (51) account for nearly half. Western Europe has 229 cases.

Europe-wide, sector breadth of rising insolvencies is softening. 43% of 216 monitored sectors (93) posted a y/y rise in Q2 2026, versus 48% in Q1, 53% in Q4 2025 and over 60% on average in 2024. Construction, transport/storage and B2C services remain the most broadly affected.

In the US, the UBS Corporate Bankruptcy Monitor shows fewer than half of sectors with a rise in the first three quarters of 2026. The largest increases are in healthcare and chemicals, with many cases in real estate, construction, retail and hospitality.

About 2.7mn jobs are directly at risk each year over 2026-2027, up 180,000 from 2025 and 700,000 from 2023. That is 2.3mn from liquidations and 0.4mn from restructuring. Europe accounts for 1.6mn and North America 650k, both 13-year highs. The US is at 590k, France 268k, Germany 239k and the UK 213k.
Jobs at risk equal 8% of the unemployed in the US and 6% in Europe. By country the share ranges from 1% in Spain and 4% in Italy to 8% in Germany and 10% in both France and the UK.

Baseline forecast: the Global Insolvency Index rises +1% in 2027 (+1pp vs the previous estimate), then falls -1% in 2028. The index would stay 22% above the 2016-2019 average and about 3% below GFC levels, a plateau at a high level rather than a recovery.

Drivers of the elevated plateau are the Middle East energy shock spillovers, higher-for-longer rates, tariff-driven trade fragmentation, industrial reallocation away from energy-disadvantaged regions, and a split between AI-linked winners and traditional cyclical losers. The active firm stock grew about 10% between 2021 and 2025, and fewer than half of young European firms survive five years.

Regional 2027 path: US +4% to 28,800 cases, Asia-Pacific +2%, North America +3%, Western Europe -1%, Latin America -2%, CEE -0.4%, Africa -4%. Germany is flat at about 25,900, France +1% to 71,400, UK -3% to 24,800 and Belgium -2% to 11,500. Western Europe's majority of countries sit in a -3%/+3% range.

Forecast revisions: North America 2027 moved from -4% to +3%, and Latin America from -7% to -2%. The US 2027 call moved from -3% to +4%, and the 2026 US call from +9% to +12%. US cases are projected at 27,700 in 2026, 28,800 in 2027 and 29,200 in 2028, about 25% above the pre-pandemic average of 23,500 and the highest since 2011.

Rates: 60% of countries will keep higher policy rates in 2027 than in the prior 12-24 months. 16% of US sectors (13 of 81) and 25% of European sectors (21 of 84) already have an interest coverage ratio below 3. A 400bps rate shock in the US or 300bps in Europe would push the remaining sectors below 3. Fewer than one in two US SMEs is profitable.

A +100bps rise in bank lending rates adds EUR6bn to EUR10bn in interest expense in Western Europe and compresses margins by 0.3pp to 0.9pp of gross value added. By country: Germany -0.3pp, UK -0.5pp, Spain -0.6pp, France -0.7pp. Added interest expense is +6bn in Spain, +7bn Germany, +8bn UK and +10bn in both Italy and France.

Energy: the 60% rise in energy costs since January 2026 cuts net margins by about 17pps in air transport (US and Europe), 15pps in US road transport and 10pps in European road transport. European chemicals lose 4pps (US 2pps) and metals and mining 3pps (US 2pps). Agriculture, retail, pharma and construction lose 1-3pps. These are upper bounds.

AI and insolvencies are uncorrelated in aggregate (66 sector-country observations across 8 European economies and 9 sectors). Belgium and Sweden, the highest adopters at about 35%, show a positive correlation of about +0.55 between AI intensity and worse insolvency trends. Information and communication, at 70% adoption, is a possible early indicator.

Downside scenario: a collapse of the AI boom resembling the dot-com burst, if it started at the end of 2026, would add about 9,300 insolvencies in 2027 in the US and Western Europe (+4,000 US, +5,300 Western Europe).

Country specifics: France reaches a record of about 71,000 cases in 2026 (+3%). Switzerland hits a record 15,000 (+32%), driven largely by a new insolvency framework in force since 2025. Germany rises +8% to 25,900, the highest since 2013. The UK falls -4% to 25,600. Australia reaches a record of about 11,850, South Korea about 2,560 and Finland 4,100.

Other regions: Brazil +6% to about 4,220 cases in 2026, the highest since 2003. Japan +6% to about 10,900 in 2026, then about 11,100 in 2027, the highest since 2012. Türkiye +31% to 2,800, the highest since 2020. Hungary -21% to about 11,300 as its 2024-2025 spike unwinds. Canada falls to 4,630 in 2026 and 4,320 in 2027.

sector_views.rationale: It accounts for 15-20% of national insolvency counts and combines high rates, weak household demand, firm fragmentation, working-capital intensity and skill shortages. It is among the most broadly affected sectors across Europe.

B2C firms face weak consumer demand and high operating costs, and they make up an average 45% of firms in Europe. They are cited as a major insolvency contributor in the US, France, the UK, Germany and Latin America.
The 60% rise in energy costs since January 2026 cuts net margins by about 17pps in air transport and 10-15pps in road transport.
European chemicals lose 4pps of margin and metals and mining 3pps, more than US peers (2pps each), under high energy costs.

It is the most AI-intensive sector at 70% adoption. It shows worse insolvency performance than the national average in five of eight countries in one reading, though another reading says it outperforms in five of eight.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Fourth consecutive annual rise, slowing from +6% in 2025 and +10% in 2024, and 21% above the 2016-2019 average.
A plateau at a high level, with the index 22% above pre-pandemic norms. 2028 would be the first year without a meaningful increase since 2022.
The US is the main driver of the global rise. Levels are about 25% above the pre-pandemic average and the highest since 2011.
Official figures showed a clear upside and drove the upward revision to the 2026 forecast.

macro_indicators.indicator: Major insolvencies (turnover above EUR50mn), year to date
macro_indicators.interpretation: A record, 38 above the 2024 peak, signalling stress among large firms and supplier-network contagion risk.
A sharp margin hit for transportation and energy-intensive industries.
The regional index reaches its GFC peak and stays 33% above pre-pandemic averages. A plateau rather than a true downturn.

macro_indicators.reading: 60% of countries hold higher policy rates in 2027 than in the prior 12-24 months
macro_indicators.interpretation: Funding costs stay elevated and margins stay squeezed, with little relief for fragile firms.

risk_factors: Higher-for-longer interest rates: 16% of US and 25% of European sectors have an interest coverage ratio below 3, and shocks of 400bps (US) or 300bps (Europe) would push the rest below that level.
Energy costs up 60% since January 2026 hit transport and energy-intensive European industry hardest.
A collapse of the AI-driven boom, comparable to the dot-com burst, would add about 9,300 insolvencies in the US and Western Europe in 2027.
Large-company failures could spread through supplier and subcontractor networks and raise insolvencies among smaller firms.
Trade fragmentation and tariffs weigh on growth, and fiscal support is limited.
The growing stock of young, fragile firms (fewer than half survive five years in Europe) and the weakness of construction keep insolvencies high without a cyclical shock.
Counterparty and supply-chain risk from buyer and supplier insolvencies stays high across most economies.
charts_described: Figure 6 shows the quarterly count of major insolvencies globally by turnover band, with Q3 2026 at 129 cases and the year-to-date total of 376 a record.
Figure 9 shows the Global Insolvency Index level (basis 100 in 2015) at 146 in 2026 (nearer 152-154 in 2027-2028 per the appendix), versus an average of 2000-2025.
geopolitical: Enduring tensions and spillovers from the Middle East energy shock keep energy costs high and weigh on global GDP growth.
Trade fragmentation from tariffs and geopolitical conflict is cited as a structural insolvency driver, along with industrial reallocation away from energy-disadvantaged regions.
The war in Ukraine's shockwaves are cited as part of the backlog of 'missing' insolvencies in Western Europe. Russia's insolvencies are forecast to rise +14% in both 2026 and 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: At the aggregate level AI adoption and insolvencies are uncorrelated across 66 sector-country observations, and macro and sector fundamentals dominate. In large mature ecosystems such as Germany and the Netherlands, AI reinforces established firms.
tension_points.bear_case: In smaller markets such as Belgium and Sweden (about 35% adoption), AI intensity correlates positively (r about +0.55) with worse insolvency trends. A collapse of the AI boom would add about 9,300 insolvencies in the US and Western Europe in 2027.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A dot-com-style collapse of the AI-driven boom starting at the end of 2026 would invalidate the benign aggregate read.

tension_points.bull_case: Growth is decelerating (+10% in 2024, +6% in 2025, +5% in 2026), the breadth of rising sectors is falling in Europe, and the index is forecast to edge down -1% in 2028.
tension_points.bear_case: Levels stay 22% above pre-pandemic norms in 2027-2028. Large-company failures are at a record, and rates and energy costs remain high.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rate shock of 400bps in the US or 300bps in Europe would push the remaining sectors below an interest coverage ratio of 3.

theme_stances.key_argument: Insolvencies keep rising in 2026, plateau in 2027 and edge down only slightly in 2028, staying well above pre-pandemic levels.
theme_stances.evidence: We do not expect a meaningful decline in business insolvencies anytime soon.

theme_stances.key_argument: Persistent high rates strain refinancing for fragile firms, notably SMEs and high-risk sectors.
theme_stances.evidence: Higher-for-longer interest rates are choking the most vulnerable firms.

theme_stances.key_argument: The 60% rise in energy costs since January 2026 hits transportation and energy-intensive European industry hardest.
theme_stances.evidence: Higher-for-longer energy costs also maintain the pressure on margins.
